title: Ἀθήνη ἐν Ἰθάκῃ
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Athena binds on her golden sandals, takes up her heavy spear and drops from the peaks of Olympus to the doorway of Odysseus' house in Ithaca, in the likeness of Mentes, a Taphian chieftain. She finds the suitors at a board game before the door, waited on by heralds and servants, eating their way through another man's stores. Telemachus, sitting unhappily among them and imagining his father's return, is the first to see the stranger; ashamed that a guest should be left standing, he takes her hand, relieves her of her spear, leads her in and seats her apart from the crowd. When the suitors have eaten and the singer Phemius has struck up, Telemachus leans close and asks who the stranger is, complaining bitterly of the men who are devouring his father's living. Athena answers that she is Mentes son of Anchialus, lord of the Taphians and a guest-friend of the house from Laertes' time, who has put in with a cargo of iron on her way to Temese for bronze. Then, disclaiming any gift of prophecy, she tells him that Odysseus is alive, held back on an island, and will find a way home — and asks in turn whether this tall young man is really his son.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
ἀμβρόσια χρύσεια, τά μιν φέρον ἠμὲν ἐφ’ ὑγρὴν
ἠδ’ ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν ἅμα πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipous’ hypo possin edēsato kala pedila,
ambrosia chryseia, ta min pheron ēmen eph’ hygrēn
ēd’ ep’ apeirona gaian hama pnoiēis anemoio·
sentences.i: So she spoke, and bound beneath her feet her fair sandals, immortal and golden, which bore her over the water and over the boundless earth alike, keeping pace with the breath of the wind;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ is ὣς εἰποῦσα, elided, the feminine aorist participle; a verse of this shape regularly follows a speech. ποσσίν is the epic dative plural of πούς (Attic ποσί), with the double σ the verse wants. ἐδήσατο is the aorist middle of δέω 'bind', middle because she binds them on herself. τά is the article-form used as a relative, 'which'. φέρον is an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἔφερον). ὑγρήν is a feminine adjective standing alone, 'the wet', for the sea, set against γαῖαν. ἠμέν … ἠδέ is the epic 'both … and'. πνοιῇς has Ionic η for Attic long α (πνοιαῖς); ἀνέμοιο is a genitive in -οιο.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος, ἀκαχμένον ὀξέι χαλκῷ,
βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρόν, τῷ δάμνησι στίχας ἀνδρῶν
ἡρώων, τοῖσίν τε κοτέσσεται ὀβριμοπάτρη.
sentences.tr:
heileto d’ alkimon enchos, akachmenon oxei chalkōi,
brithy mega stibaron, tōi damnēsi stichas andrōn
hērōōn, toisin te kotessetai obrimopatrē.
sentences.l:
and she took up her strong spear, tipped with sharp bronze,
heavy, huge, massive, with which she overpowers the ranks of men,
of heroes, with whomever she is angered, she of the mighty father.
sentences.i: and she took up her strong spear, tipped with sharp bronze, heavy and huge and massive, with which she beats down the ranks of men, of heroes, with whomever she, the daughter of a mighty father, is angered.
sentences.n: εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω, 'took up for herself'. ἄλκιμον is 'strong in defence', from ἀλκή. ἀκαχμένον is a perfect passive participle of obscure formation, 'sharpened'. ὀξέι is the uncontracted dative of ὀξύς (Attic ὀξεῖ). βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρόν stand without a connective. τῷ is a relative dative of the instrument. δάμνησι is the third singular of δάμνημι 'overpower', with the ending -ησι. ἡρώων is held over to the head of 101, in apposition to ἀνδρῶν. τοῖσιν is a relative dative, and τε marks a general truth, with the short-vowel aorist subjunctive κοτέσσεται of κοτέομαι 'bear a grudge'. ὀβριμοπάτρη is ὄβριμος with πατήρ, a title of Athena alone.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀίξασα,
στῆ δ’ Ἰθάκης ἐνὶ δήμῳ ἐπὶ προθύροις Ὀδυσῆος,
οὐδοῦ ἐπ’ αὐλείου·
sentences.tr:
bē de kat’ Oulympoio karēnōn aixasa,
stē d’ Ithakēs eni dēmōi epi prothyrois Odysēos,
oudou ep’ auleiou·
sentences.i: She went darting down from the peaks of Olympus and stood in the land of Ithaca at the forecourt of Odysseus, upon the threshold of the court;
sentences.n: βῆ and στῆ are unaugmented root aorists of βαίνω and ἵστημι (Attic ἔβη, ἔστη). Οὐλύμποιο has the epic Οὐ- for Ὀ-, which gives the verse a long first syllable, and a genitive in -οιο. κάρηνα are properly 'heads', so the peaks of the mountain. ἀίξασα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω 'dart'. δῆμος is a district and the people in it, so 'in the land of Ithaca'. τὰ πρόθυρα are the gateway and the space before the house door. In οὐδοῦ ἐπ’ αὐλείου the preposition stands after its noun; αὔλειος is the adjective of αὐλή, the walled courtyard. The sentence stops in the middle of 104.

sentences.t:
παλάμῃ δ’ ἔχε χάλκεον ἔγχος,
εἰδομένη ξείνῳ, Ταφίων ἡγήτορι Μέντῃ.
sentences.tr:
palamēi d’ eche chalkeon enchos,
eidomenē xeinōi, Taphiōn hēgētori Mentēi.
sentences.l:
and in her palm she held the bronze spear,
having made herself like a stranger, like Mentes, the Taphians' leader.
sentences.i: and in her hand she held the bronze spear, having made herself like a stranger, like Mentes, the leader of the Taphians.
sentences.n: παλάμῃ is a dative of place, 'in her palm'. ἔχε is an unaugmented imperfect. χάλκεον is uncontracted (Attic χαλκοῦν). εἰδομένη is the middle participle of εἴδομαι 'make oneself like, appear as', and it takes the dative of what is resembled: ξείνῳ, then Μέντῃ in apposition. ξεῖνος is the epic ξένος, and the word means both 'stranger' and 'guest-friend'; the two senses run together through the whole scene. Μέντῃ is the dative of a first-declension masculine. The Taphians are seafarers of the islands off Acarnania. The narrator goes on calling the disguised goddess 'she'.

sentences.t: εὗρε δ’ ἄρα μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας.
sentences.tr: heure d’ ara mnēstēras agēnoras.
sentences.l: And she found the lordly suitors.
sentences.i: And so she found the lordly suitors.
sentences.n: εὗρε keeps its augment. ἄρα, 'so, as it turned out', presents what she came upon. μνηστῆρες, from μνάομαι 'woo', are the suitors Athena spoke of at 1.91; this is the first sight of them. ἀγήνωρ is usually derived from ἄγαν and ἀνήρ, 'very manly'; in the Odyssey the word leans towards 'overbearing', and 'lordly' is kept for it every time it comes. The sentence is a half-line and ends with a full stop in the middle of the verse, as at 1.19.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα
πεσσοῖσι προπάροιθε θυράων θυμὸν ἔτερπον
ἥμενοι ἐν ῥινοῖσι βοῶν, οὓς ἔκτανον αὐτοί·
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeita
pessoisi proparoithe thyraōn thymon eterpon
hēmenoi en rhinoisi boōn, hous ektanon autoi·
sentences.i: They were delighting themselves with draughts before the doors, sitting on the hides of cattle which they had killed themselves;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν is the pronoun, 'they', and is answered by κήρυκες δέ at 109. πεσσοί are the pieces of a board game; what the game was is not known, and 'draughts' is no more than a convenience. προπάροιθε takes the genitive θυράων, a first-declension genitive plural in -άων (Attic θυρῶν). θυμὸν ἔτερπον has an accusative of the part affected, 'delighted their heart'. ἥμενοι is the participle of ἧμαι 'sit'. ῥινοί are ox-hides. ἔκτανον is the aorist of κτείνω, here with its augment, and αὐτοί is pointed: the killing is their own doing, and the cattle are not theirs.

sentences.t:
κήρυκες δ’ αὐτοῖσι καὶ ὀτρηροὶ θεράποντες
οἱ μὲν οἶνον ἔμισγον ἐνὶ κρητῆρσι καὶ ὕδωρ,
οἱ δ’ αὖτε σπόγγοισι πολυτρήτοισι τραπέζας
νίζον καὶ πρότιθεν, τοὶ δὲ κρέα πολλὰ δατεῦντο.
sentences.tr:
kērykes d’ autoisi kai otrēroi therapontes
hoi men oinon emisgon eni krētērsi kai hydōr,
hoi d’ aute spongoisi polytrētoisi trapezas
nizon kai protithen, toi de krea polla dateunto.
sentences.l:
And heralds for them, and busy attendants —
some were mixing wine in the bowls, and water,
and others again with sponges full-of-holes the tables
were washing and setting out, and others were portioning much meat.
sentences.i: Heralds and busy attendants were waiting on them: some mixed wine and water in the bowls, others washed the tables with many-holed sponges and set them out, and others portioned out great quantities of meat.
sentences.n: κήρυκες δ’ αὐτοῖσι has no verb of its own; the three clauses οἱ μέν … οἱ δέ … τοὶ δέ divide the heralds and attendants into groups. αὐτοῖσι is a dative of the persons served. ὀτρηροί is 'quick, busy', of the family of ὀτρύνω. ἔμισγον keeps its augment and νίζον beside it is an unaugmented imperfect, and πρότιθεν is προετίθεσαν with the shorter third-plural ending -εν. τοί is the article-form as a pronoun, 'they'. πολύτρητος is 'much-pierced', which is what a sponge is. δατεῦντο is δατέοντο contracted in the Ionic way, the imperfect middle of δατέομαι 'divide'. Wine was drunk mixed with water in a κρητήρ, and the mixing opens a meal.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ πολὺ πρῶτος ἴδε Τηλέμαχος θεοειδής,
sentences.tr: tēn de poly prōtos ide Tēlemachos theoeidēs,
sentences.l: And her by far the first to see was Telemachus, godlike-in-form,
sentences.i: Telemachus, godlike in form, was far the first to see her,
sentences.n: τήν is the pronoun, 'her'; the narrator keeps the feminine for Athena, although what Telemachus sees is a man. πολὺ πρῶτος has an adverbial accusative with the adjective, 'first by a long way'. ἴδε is the unaugmented aorist of the root of εἶδον. Telemachus is named here for the first time; at 1.88 Athena called him only 'his son'. θεοειδής is θεός with εἶδος, 'of the form of a god', and is kept distinct from ἀντίθεος 'godlike' at 1.21 and 1.70. The line ends in a comma and the sentence runs on to the end of 117, which is why it is cut here.

sentences.t:
ἧστο γὰρ ἐν μνηστῆρσι φίλον τετιημένος ἦτορ,
ὀσσόμενος πατέρ’ ἐσθλὸν ἐνὶ φρεσίν, εἴ ποθεν ἐλθὼν
μνηστήρων τῶν μὲν σκέδασιν κατὰ δώματα θείη,
τιμὴν δ’ αὐτὸς ἔχοι καὶ δώμασιν οἷσιν ἀνάσσοι.
sentences.tr:
hēsto gar en mnēstērsi philon tetiēmenos ētor,
ossomenos pater’ esthlon eni phresin, ei pothen elthōn
mnēstērōn tōn men skedasin kata dōmata theiē,
timēn d’ autos echoi kai dōmasin hoisin anassoi.
sentences.l:
for he was sitting among the suitors, grieved in his own heart,
seeing his noble father in his mind, if from somewhere he might come
and of these suitors make a scattering throughout the halls,
and himself hold the honour and be lord over his own house.
sentences.i: for he was sitting among the suitors with grief in his heart, seeing his noble father in his mind: if only he might come from somewhere and make a scattering of these suitors through the halls, and hold the honour himself and be lord of his own house.
sentences.n: ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι. τετιημένος is the perfect participle of a defective verb, 'grieved, downcast', with φίλον ἦτορ as an accusative of respect; φίλος with a part of the body does duty for 'his own', as at 1.60. ὀσσόμενος, from ὄσσομαι 'see before one', governs πατέρ’ ἐσθλόν. εἰ with the optatives θείη, ἔχοι, ἀνάσσοι states what he hopes for. σκέδασιν … θείη is a periphrasis for σκεδάσειε, 'make a scattering'. μνηστήρων τῶν is 'of those suitors', with the pronoun after its noun. δώμασιν οἷσιν is the possessive ὅς, 'his own house', and ἀνάσσω takes the dative.

sentences.t: τὰ φρονέων, μνηστῆρσι μεθήμενος, εἴσιδ’ Ἀθήνην.
sentences.tr: ta phroneōn, mnēstērsi methēmenos, eisid’ Athēnēn.
sentences.l: Thinking these things, sitting among the suitors, he caught sight of Athena.
sentences.i: With these thoughts in him, as he sat among the suitors, he caught sight of Athena.
sentences.n: τά is the pronoun, 'these things', the object of φρονέων, which is uncontracted (Attic φρονῶν). μεθήμενος is the participle of μέθημαι 'sit among', with the dative. εἴσιδ’ is εἴσιδε elided, the aorist of εἰσοράω. The narrator names Ἀθήνην outright: the reader is told who the stranger is, and Telemachus is not. The full stop at the end of 117 has closed the long sentence; this line begins again and gathers up both of its ideas, his thoughts and his seat among the suitors, in that order.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰθὺς προθύροιο, νεμεσσήθη δ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ξεῖνον δηθὰ θύρῃσιν ἐφεστάμεν·
sentences.tr:
bē d’ ithys prothyroio, nemessēthē d’ eni thymōi
xeinon dētha thyrēisin ephestamen·
sentences.l:
And he went straight towards the forecourt, and was indignant in his heart
that a stranger should stand long at the doors;
sentences.i: He went straight to the forecourt, indignant at heart that a stranger should be left standing so long at the doors;
sentences.n: βῆ is again the unaugmented aorist of 102. ἰθύς is the epic εὐθύς, here a preposition with the genitive, 'straight towards'; προθύροιο is a genitive in -οιο. νεμεσσήθη is the aorist passive of νεμεσάω, with the double σ of the verse: νέμεσις is the feeling that something improper is being done. The infinitive ἐφεστάμεν, the perfect of ἐφίστημι in -μεν (Attic ἐφεστάναι), with its accusative subject ξεῖνον gives the ground of that feeling. θύρῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσι. δηθά is 'for long', the adverb used at 1.49. To leave a guest at the door is a failure of the host.

sentences.t:
ἐγγύθι δὲ στὰς
χεῖρ’ ἕλε δεξιτερὴν καὶ ἐδέξατο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
engythi de stas
cheir’ hele dexiterēn kai edexato chalkeon enchos,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
and standing close by
he took her right hand and received the bronze spear,
and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and standing close he took her right hand and relieved her of the bronze spear, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι. δεξιτερός is the epic δεξιός. ἕλε is unaugmented (Attic εἷλε) and ἐδέξατο beside it keeps the augment: the two stand in one line. Taking the guest's spear is the host's act, and the weapon is given up before the man is seated. φωνήσας is 'having raised his voice'. μιν is 'her', the narrator's feminine again, though Telemachus is addressing a man. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the poem's commonest introduction to a speech; πτερόεις, from πτερόν 'feather, wing', is 'winged', and the image of words flying from speaker to hearer is kept in both English layers.

sentences.t: χαῖρε, ξεῖνε, παρ’ ἄμμι φιλήσεαι·
sentences.tr: chaire, xeine, par’ ammi philēseai·
sentences.l: “Welcome, stranger; among us you will be befriended;
sentences.i: “Welcome, stranger. Among us you will be treated as a friend;
sentences.n: χαῖρε is the imperative of χαίρω 'rejoice', the ordinary Greek word of greeting, and 'welcome' is kept for it. ξεῖνε is the vocative of ξεῖνος: the man is a stranger, and from this moment a guest. ἄμμι is the epic dative of the first person plural (Attic ἡμῖν). φιλήσεαι is an uncontracted second singular future of φιλέω (Attic φιλήσῃ), middle or passive in form; φιλέω in Homer is not only 'love' but 'treat as a φίλος', that is, give a guest everything a guest is owed. Murray prints no quotation marks, so the English layers supply them.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
δείπνου πασσάμενος μυθήσεαι ὅττεό σε χρή.
sentences.tr:
autar epeita
deipnou passamenos mythēseai hotteo se chrē.
sentences.l:
but afterwards,
when you have partaken of a meal, you shall say what you need.”
sentences.i: and afterwards, when you have had your meal, you shall tell us what you need.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα is the epic 'but afterwards'. πασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of πατέομαι 'partake of', with the genitive δείπνου. μυθήσεαι is another uncontracted future middle (Attic μυθήσῃ), from μυθέομαι 'speak'. ὅττεο is the epic genitive of ὅ τι (Attic οὗτινος), governed by χρή, which in Homer takes an accusative of the person and a genitive of the thing: 'what there is need of for you'. The order of hospitality is fixed — food first, questions after — and the poem keeps to it: the questions come only at 169.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἡγεῖθ’, ἡ δ’ ἕσπετο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn hēgeith’, hē d’ hespeto Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: So having spoken he led the way, and she followed, Pallas Athena.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and led the way, and Pallas Athena followed.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is the masculine of the participle used of the goddess at 96. ἡγεῖθ’ is ἡγεῖτο, the imperfect of ἡγέομαι 'lead', elided and aspirated before ἡ. ἡ δέ is the pronoun, 'and she'. ἕσπετο is the aorist of ἕπομαι 'follow'. Παλλάς is a title of Athena whose meaning is not known; the ancients connected it with πάλλω 'brandish', or with a companion of that name. The host walks in front and the guest comes after, and the goddess takes the guest's place.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἔντοσθεν ἔσαν δόμου ὑψηλοῖο,
ἔγχος μέν ῥ’ ἔστησε φέρων πρὸς κίονα μακρὴν
δουροδόκης ἔντοσθεν ἐυξόου, ἔνθα περ ἄλλα
ἔγχε’ Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος ἵστατο πολλά,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē rh’ entosthen esan domou hypsēloio,
enchos men rh’ estēse pherōn pros kiona makrēn
dourodokēs entosthen eyxoou, entha per alla
enche’ Odyssēos talasiphronos histato polla,
sentences.l:
And when they were inside the high house,
the spear he carried and set against a tall pillar,
inside a well-planed spear-stand, in the very place where other
spears of Odysseus the enduring-minded stood, many of them,
sentences.i: When they were inside the high house, he carried the spear and set it against a tall pillar, inside a well-planed spear-stand, in the very place where many other spears of steadfast Odysseus were standing,
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is the pronoun, 'and they'; ὅτε δή ῥα is 'when in fact', with ῥα the worn-down ἄρα. ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν, as at 1.12, and δόμου ὑψηλοῖο a genitive in -οιο after ἔντοσθεν. ἔστησε is the transitive aorist of ἵστημι 'set up', against the intransitive ἵστατο in 129, 'were standing'. κίων is feminine here. δουροδόκη is δόρυ 'spear-shaft' with δέχομαι, the rack that receives them. ἐυξόου is ἐυ- with ξέω 'plane'; the archive prints ἐυ- without a diaeresis. ἔγχε’ is uncontracted ἔγχεα. ταλασίφρων belongs with τλῆναι 'endure' and is one of three epithets of Odysseus in -φρων, each kept distinct.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴν δ’ ἐς θρόνον εἷσεν ἄγων, ὑπὸ λῖτα πετάσσας,
καλὸν δαιδάλεον·
sentences.tr:
autēn d’ es thronon heisen agōn, hypo lita petassas,
kalon daidaleon·
sentences.l:
and her he led and seated on a chair, having spread a linen cloth beneath,
a fine chair, cunningly-worked;
sentences.i: and he led her to a chair and seated her there, a fine chair of cunning work, spreading a linen cloth beneath her;
sentences.n: αὐτήν, 'her', answers ἔγχος μέν at 127: the spear goes one way, the guest another. εἷσεν is the transitive aorist of ἵζω 'seat'. ἄγων is a participle of accompanying action, 'leading her'. λῖτα is the accusative of λίς, a smooth linen cloth spread over the seat, and πετάσσας the aorist participle of πετάννυμι 'spread out'. καλὸν δαιδάλεον are masculine and belong to θρόνον, not to the neuter λῖτα. δαιδάλεος is 'worked with skill', of the family of δαίδαλον. A θρόνος is the high chair with a footstool, the seat of honour.

sentences.t: ὑπὸ δὲ θρῆνυς ποσὶν ἦεν.
sentences.tr: hypo de thrēnys posin ēen.
sentences.l: and beneath, for her feet, was a footstool.
sentences.i: and beneath it there was a footstool for her feet.
sentences.n: ὑπό is an adverb here, 'beneath', not a preposition. θρῆνυς is the footstool that goes with a θρόνος and makes it the seat of honour. ποσίν is the ordinary dative plural of πούς, beside the epic ποσσίν with double σ at 96; Homer uses both as the verse requires. ἦεν is the epic ἦν, as at 1.18. The half-line finishes the furnishing of the guest's place before the host sees to his own seat.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ αὐτὸς κλισμὸν θέτο ποικίλον, ἔκτοθεν ἄλλων
μνηστήρων, μὴ ξεῖνος ἀνιηθεὶς ὀρυμαγδῷ
δείπνῳ ἁδήσειεν, ὑπερφιάλοισι μετελθών,
ἠδ’ ἵνα μιν περὶ πατρὸς ἀποιχομένοιο ἔροιτο.
sentences.tr:
par d’ autos klismon theto poikilon, ektothen allōn
mnēstērōn, mē xeinos aniētheis orymagdōi
deipnōi hadēseien, hyperphialoisi metelthōn,
ēd’ hina min peri patros apoichomenoio eroito.
sentences.l:
And beside her he himself set an inlaid seat, away from the others,
the suitors, lest the stranger, vexed by the din,
should take no pleasure in his meal, having come among overbearing men,
and so that he might ask her about his father, gone away.
sentences.i: Beside her he set his own inlaid seat, away from the others, the suitors, so that the stranger should not be put off his meal by the uproar, finding himself among overbearing men, and so that he might ask her about his father, who was gone.
sentences.n: πάρ is πάρα (= παρά) used as an adverb, 'beside her'. θέτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of τίθημι, middle because he sets the seat for himself. A κλισμός is a lighter chair than the θρόνος he has given his guest. ἔκτοθεν takes the genitive, 'away from'. μή with the aorist optative ἁδήσειεν is a negative purpose clause after a past verb; ἀνιηθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀνιάω 'distress', ὀρυμαγδός a loud confused noise, and ἁδέω 'have had enough of'. ἵνα … ἔροιτο is a second purpose clause with the optative. ἀποιχομένοιο is a genitive in -οιο with πατρός.

sentences.t:
χέρνιβα δ’ ἀμφίπολος προχόῳ ἐπέχευε φέρουσα
καλῇ χρυσείῃ, ὑπὲρ ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος,
νίψασθαι·
sentences.tr:
cherniba d’ amphipolos prochoōi epecheue pherousa
kalēi chryseiēi, hyper argyreoio lebētos,
nipsasthai·
sentences.i: A handmaid brought water for the hands in a fine golden pitcher and poured it over a silver basin, for them to wash;
sentences.n: χέρνιψ, from χείρ and νίζω, is the water poured over the hands before a meal. ἀμφίπολος is a woman in attendance. πρόχοος is the jug it is poured from, and its adjectives καλῇ χρυσείῃ follow at the head of 137; χρυσείῃ is uncontracted (Attic χρυσῇ). ἐπέχευε is the aorist of ἐπιχέω, the stem that comes again in ἔχευαν at 146, with its augment inside the compound (ἐπ-έ-χευε). ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος is a genitive in -οιο, the basin that catches what is poured. νίψασθαι is an aorist middle infinitive of purpose, 'for washing themselves'. Gold and silver are the ordinary furniture of a great house in the poem.

sentences.t: παρὰ δὲ ξεστὴν ἐτάνυσσε τράπεζαν.
sentences.tr: para de xestēn etanysse trapezan.
sentences.l: and beside them she drew up a polished table.
sentences.i: and she drew a polished table up beside them.
sentences.n: παρά is an adverb here, 'alongside'. ξεστήν is 'planed smooth', from ξέω, the verb behind ἐυξόου at 128. ἐτάνυσσε is the aorist of τανύω 'stretch, draw out', with the double σ the verse wants. Each diner has his own small table, drawn up to his seat when he eats and taken away afterwards; there is no single board for the company.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δ’ αἰδοίη ταμίη παρέθηκε φέρουσα,
εἴδατα πόλλ’ ἐπιθεῖσα, χαριζομένη παρεόντων·
sentences.tr:
siton d’ aidoiē tamiē parethēke pherousa,
eidata poll’ epitheisa, charizomenē pareontōn·
sentences.l:
And bread a revered housekeeper set beside them, bringing it,
and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what was at hand;
sentences.i: A revered housekeeper brought bread and set it beside them, and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what she had by her;
sentences.n: σῖτος is bread or grain, the staple of a meal, as against κρέα 'meat'. αἰδοίη is 'to be held in respect', from αἰδώς; it is used of people whose place gives them a claim to regard, and it goes with the office rather than the scene. ταμίη is the woman who has charge of the stores (Attic ταμία), with Ionic η for long α. παρέθηκε is the aorist of παρατίθημι. εἴδατα are cooked dishes. χαριζομένη takes the genitive παρεόντων (uncontracted, Attic παρόντων), 'being free with what was there'. The serving follows a fixed order: washing, bread, meat, cups, wine.

sentences.t:
δαιτρὸς δὲ κρειῶν πίνακας παρέθηκεν ἀείρας
παντοίων, παρὰ δέ σφι τίθει χρύσεια κύπελλα·
sentences.tr:
daitros de kreiōn pinakas parethēken aeiras
pantoiōn, para de sphi tithei chryseia kypella·
sentences.l:
and a carver lifted and set beside them platters of meats
of all kinds, and beside them was setting golden cups;
sentences.i: and a carver lifted platters of meats of every kind and set them by, and was putting golden cups at their side;
sentences.n: δαιτρός, from δαίομαι 'divide', is the man whose office is to carve and portion, the work the attendants were doing at 112. κρειῶν is the epic genitive plural of κρέας, with epic ει for ε (Attic κρεῶν), with παντοίων held over to the head of 142, as ἡρώων was at 101. πίναξ is a wooden platter. ἀείρας is the aorist participle of ἀείρω (Attic αἴρω) 'lift'. σφι is the epic dative plural pronoun, 'for them'. τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι (Attic ἐτίθει). χρύσεια is uncontracted, beside χρυσείῃ at 137.

sentences.t: κῆρυξ δ’ αὐτοῖσιν θάμ’ ἐπῴχετο οἰνοχοεύων.
sentences.tr: kēryx d’ autoisin tham’ epōicheto oinochoeuōn.
sentences.l: And a herald came to them often, pouring the wine.
sentences.i: And a herald came round to them again and again, pouring the wine.
sentences.n: αὐτοῖσιν is 'to them', the two seated apart at their own table. θάμ’ is θαμά, 'often, again and again'. ἐπῴχετο is the imperfect of ἐποίχομαι 'go to and fro to'. οἰνοχοεύων is a lengthened epic form of οἰνοχοέω, οἶνος with χέω, 'pour wine'. The heralds who waited on the suitors at 109 wait on the guest too, so that the stranger at the side table is not left worse served than the crowd.

sentences.t: ἐς δ’ ἦλθον μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες.
sentences.tr: es d’ ēlthon mnēstēres agēnores.
sentences.l: And in came the lordly suitors.
sentences.i: And in came the lordly suitors.
sentences.n: ἐς δ’ ἦλθον is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from its verb: εἰσῆλθον 'they came in', with ἐς for εἰς. The half-line takes up the words μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας of 106 with the same epithet and the same break in the middle of the verse; there the goddess found them outside at their game, here they come in to eat. ἀγήνωρ is rendered 'lordly' every time, whatever the scene.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα
ἑξείης ἕζοντο κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε,
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeita
hexeiēs hezonto kata klismous te thronous te,
sentences.l:
They, then,
in order seated themselves along the seats and the chairs,
sentences.i: They then took their places in order along the seats and the chairs,
sentences.n: οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα repeats the words of 106 in the same position in the verse, the second half-line. ἑξείης is the epic ἑξῆς, 'one after another, in order'. ἕζοντο is the imperfect middle of ἕζομαι 'seat oneself'. κατά with the accusative is distributive, 'along, throughout'. κλισμοί and θρόνοι are the two kinds of seat already named, the lighter chair of 132 and the high chair of 130, each standing in its own place in the hall.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ κήρυκες μὲν ὕδωρ ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν,
σῖτον δὲ δμῳαὶ παρενήνεον ἐν κανέοισιν,
κοῦροι δὲ κρητῆρας ἐπεστέψαντο ποτοῖο.
sentences.tr:
toisi de kērykes men hydōr epi cheiras echeuan,
siton de dmōiai parenēneon en kaneoisin,
kouroi de krētēras epestepsanto potoio.
sentences.l:
and for them the heralds poured water over their hands,
and serving-women heaped up bread in baskets,
and young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink.
sentences.i: and the heralds poured water over their hands, serving-women heaped bread in baskets, and young men filled the mixing-bowls to the brim with drink.
sentences.n: τοῖσι is the pronoun, 'for them'. ἔχευαν is a third plural aorist in -αν of χέω (Attic ἔχεαν). δμῳαί are women of the household in service, the feminine of δμώς. παρενήνεον is the imperfect of παρανηνέω 'heap up beside', with its augment inside the compound (παρ-ε-νήνεον) and reduplication in the stem. κάνεον is a basket, with the dative plural in -οισι. κοῦροι, 'young men', are the servers. ἐπεστέψαντο is from στέφω 'crown': they crowned the bowls, filling them so that the drink stood level with the brim, with ποτοῖο a genitive of what filled them.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ep’ oneiath’ hetoima prokeimena cheiras iallon.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα elided, 'good things', from the root of ὀνίνημι 'profit'; of a meal it means the food. ἑτοῖμα and προκείμενα both qualify it, 'ready' and 'lying before them'. ἴαλλον is an unaugmented imperfect of ἰάλλω 'send forth', the regular verb for putting out the hand to food. The whole line is a formula that closes the serving and opens the eating.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο
μνηστῆρες, τοῖσιν μὲν ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ἄλλα μεμήλει,
μολπή τ’ ὀρχηστύς τε·
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento
mnēstēres, toisin men eni phresin alla memēlei,
molpē t’ orchēstys te·
sentences.i: But when the suitors had put from them the desire for drink and food, other things were on their minds, song and dancing;
sentences.n: The whole of 150 is the formula for the end of a meal. ἐξ … ἕντο is tmesis for ἐξέντο, the aorist middle of ἐξίημι: 'they sent the desire out of themselves', with ἔρον (= ἔρως) as its object and πόσιος and ἐδητύος as objective genitives. πόσις and ἐδητύς are abstract nouns, 'drinking' and 'eating'. μνηστῆρες is held over to the head of 151. τοῖσιν is the pronoun, 'for them'. μεμήλει is the pluperfect of μέλω used as an imperfect, 'was a care'. μολπή is singing joined with dancing; ὀρχηστύς is a noun in -τύς, like ἐδητύς above it.

sentences.t: τὰ γάρ τ’ ἀναθήματα δαιτός·
sentences.tr: ta gar t’ anathēmata daitos·
sentences.l: for these are the adornments of a feast;
sentences.i: for these are the things that crown a feast;
sentences.n: τά is the pronoun, 'these things', the song and the dancing. τε is the epic τε that marks a standing truth, as at 1.50, and γάρ τε together give the general fact behind the particular case. ἀναθήματα, from ἀνατίθημι 'set up, add', are things put on for ornament, the crowning touch; the later sense 'votive offering' is not in play. The verb 'are' is left out, as often. δαιτός is the genitive of δαίς 'feast', the word used of Poseidon's feast at 1.26.

sentences.t:
κῆρυξ δ’ ἐν χερσὶν κίθαριν περικαλλέα θῆκεν
Φημίῳ, ὅς ῥ’ ἤειδε παρὰ μνηστῆρσιν ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.tr:
kēryx d’ en chersin kitharin perikallea thēken
Phēmiōi, hos rh’ ēeide para mnēstērsin anankēi.
sentences.l:
And a herald put a very beautiful lyre into the hands
of Phemius, who sang among the suitors under compulsion.
sentences.i: And a herald put a lyre of great beauty into the hands of Phemius, who sang among the suitors under compulsion.
sentences.n: ἐν χερσίν is 'into the hands', a dative of rest where motion is meant. κίθαρις is the stringed instrument, later κιθάρα. περικαλλέα is the uncontracted accusative of περικαλλής (Attic περικαλλῆ). θῆκεν is the aorist of τίθημι. The name Φήμιος belongs with φήμη 'utterance'. ῥα is the light 'so, as it happened'. ἤειδε is the imperfect of ἀείδω, with the augment showing as η-. ἀνάγκῃ is a dative of manner, 'by compulsion': the singer belongs to the house and performs for the suitors because he has no choice, and the poem says so at once.

sentences.t: ἦ τοι ὁ φορμίζων ἀνεβάλλετο καλὸν ἀείδειν.
sentences.tr: ē toi ho phormizōn aneballeto kalon aeidein.
sentences.l: And he indeed, playing on the lyre, struck up to sing beautifully.
sentences.i: And he struck the strings and lifted up a beautiful song.
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is an affirming particle, 'and so indeed'. ὁ is the pronoun, 'he'. φορμίζων is from φόρμιγξ, the other Homeric word for the lyre, beside κίθαρις in the line before. ἀνεβάλλετο, the imperfect middle of ἀναβάλλω, is the technical word for beginning a song, 'struck up'. καλόν is an adverbial accusative with ἀείδειν, 'to sing beautifully'. What he sang is not reported: the scene turns away to the two seated apart.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχος προσέφη γλαυκῶπιν Ἀθήνην,
ἄγχι σχὼν κεφαλήν, ἵνα μὴ πευθοίαθ’ οἱ ἄλλοι·
sentences.tr:
autar Tēlemachos prosephē glaukōpin Athēnēn,
anchi schōn kephalēn, hina mē peuthoiath’ hoi alloi·
sentences.l:
But Telemachus addressed gleaming-eyed Athena,
holding his head close, so that the others should not hear:
sentences.i: But Telemachus spoke to gleaming-eyed Athena, holding his head close to hers so that the others should not hear:
sentences.n: αὐτάρ turns from the hall to the pair at their own table. προσέφη is the imperfect of πρόσφημι 'address', the verb of the reply-formula at 1.63, and it takes its object in the accusative. γλαυκῶπιν Ἀθήνην is the fixed pair of 1.44 and 1.80 in the accusative, kept as 'gleaming-eyed Athena' every time; the exact sense of γλαυκῶπις is uncertain. ἄγχι σχών is 'having held close', from ἔχω. ἵνα μή with the optative πευθοίαθ’ (πευθοίατο, an epic third plural middle for πυνθάνοιντο) is a negative purpose clause after a past verb, like μή … ἁδήσειεν at 134.

sentences.t: ξεῖνε φίλ’, ἦ καί μοι νεμεσήσεαι ὅττι κεν εἴπω;
sentences.tr: xeine phil’, ē kai moi nemesēseai hotti ken eipō;
sentences.l: “Dear stranger, will you really be indignant with me at whatever I say?
sentences.i: “Dear stranger, will you take it amiss, whatever I may say?
sentences.n: ξεῖνε φίλ’ is φίλε elided; φίλος is 'dear' here, a warm address to the guest he has just taken in. ἦ is the particle that makes a question earnest, 'really'. νεμεσήσεαι is an uncontracted second singular future middle (Attic νεμεσήσῃ), from the verb of Telemachus' own indignation at 119; he asks the stranger not to feel what he felt himself. ὅττι is the epic ὅ τι 'whatever'; κε is the epic ἄν, and with the aorist subjunctive εἴπω the clause is indefinite. The politeness is not empty: what he is about to say is a complaint about his own house.

sentences.t:
τούτοισιν μὲν ταῦτα μέλει, κίθαρις καὶ ἀοιδή,
ῥεῖ’, ἐπεὶ ἀλλότριον βίοτον νήποινον ἔδουσιν,
ἀνέρος, οὗ δή που λεύκ’ ὀστέα πύθεται ὄμβρῳ
κείμεν’ ἐπ’ ἠπείρου, ἢ εἰν ἁλὶ κῦμα κυλίνδει.
sentences.tr:
toutoisin men tauta melei, kitharis kai aoidē,
rhei’, epei allotrion bioton nēpoinon edousin,
aneros, hou dē pou leuk’ ostea pythetai ombrōi
keimen’ ep’ ēpeirou, ē ein hali kyma kylindei.
sentences.l:
To these men these things are a care, the lyre and song,
easily, since another man's living they devour unpunished,
a man whose white bones, I suppose, are rotting in the rain
as they lie on dry land, or the wave rolls them in the sea.
sentences.i: These men care for this and nothing else, the lyre and song — easily enough, since they devour another man's living and pay nothing for it, a man whose white bones, I suppose, are rotting in the rain where they lie on dry land, or else the wave is rolling them in the sea.
sentences.n: τούτοισιν is a dative plural of οὗτος with μέλει 'is a care', taking up μεμήλει at 151; ταῦτα is the subject and κίθαρις καὶ ἀοιδή stand in apposition to it. ῥεῖα (elided ῥεῖ’) is 'easily', thrown to the head of its line for weight. βίοτος is the substance a man lives on. νήποινος is νη- 'not' with ποινή 'requital', 'without paying for it'. ἀνέρος is the epic genitive of ἀνήρ (Attic ἀνδρός), and οὗ the relative. δή που is 'I suppose', a guess and not knowledge. πύθεται is the present of πύθομαι 'rot'. κείμεν’ is κείμενα, with uncontracted ὀστέα. εἰν is the epic ἐν before a vowel.

sentences.t:
εἰ κεῖνόν γ’ Ἰθάκηνδε ἰδοίατο νοστήσαντα,
πάντες κ’ ἀρησαίατ’ ἐλαφρότεροι πόδας εἶναι
ἢ ἀφνειότεροι χρυσοῖό τε ἐσθῆτός τε.
sentences.tr:
ei keinon g’ Ithakēnde idoiato nostēsanta,
pantes k’ arēsaiat’ elaphroteroi podas einai
ē aphneioteroi chrysoio te esthētos te.
sentences.l:
If they were to see that man come home to Ithaca,
they would all pray to be lighter in their feet
rather than richer in gold and in clothing.
sentences.i: If they were to see that man come home to Ithaca, every one of them would pray to be lighter on his feet rather than richer in gold and clothing.
sentences.n: κεῖνον is ἐκεῖνον, 'that man'; the father is still not named in this speech. Ἰθάκηνδε has the suffix -δε 'to', as at 1.88. ἰδοίατο and ἀρησαίατ’ are epic third plural optatives in -ατο (Attic ἴδοιντο, ἀράσαιντο), and κε is the epic ἄν, so the sentence is a less vivid future condition. νοστήσαντα is the participle of νοστέω, the verb of νόστος. ἐλαφρότεροι πόδας is a comparative with an accusative of respect, 'lighter as to the feet'. ἀφνειότεροι takes the genitive of what one is rich in. The wish is grim: they would want speed to run, not wealth.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὁ μὲν ὣς ἀπόλωλε κακὸν μόρον, οὐδέ τις ἡμῖν
θαλπωρή, εἴ πέρ τις ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων
φῇσιν ἐλεύσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ ho men hōs apolōle kakon moron, oude tis hēmin
thalpōrē, ei per tis epichthoniōn anthrōpōn
phēisin eleusesthai·
sentences.i: But as things are, he has perished so, by an evil fate, and no warmth of comfort is left us, even if some man upon the earth says that he is coming;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ is 'but as it is', the regular turn from what might have been back to fact. ὁ μέν is the pronoun, 'he'. ὥς, accented, is 'in that way', distinct from unaccented ὡς 'as'. ἀπόλωλε is the perfect of ἀπόλλυμι, 'has perished and is gone'. κακὸν μόρον is an inner accusative of the fate met; μόρος is a man's portion, the word of ὑπὲρ μόρον at 1.34. θαλπωρή, from θάλπω 'warm', is the warmth of comfort, with 'is' left out. φῇσιν is the third singular subjunctive of φημί with the ending -σι(ν), like ἔλθῃσι at 1.77. ἐπιχθόνιος is 'upon the earth', an epithet of mortals as against the gods.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ὤλετο νόστιμον ἦμαρ.
sentences.tr: tou d’ ōleto nostimon ēmar.
sentences.l: and for him the homecoming day has perished.
sentences.i: and the day of his homecoming is gone.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the pronoun, a genitive of the person, 'his'. ὤλετο is the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι and keeps its augment, beside the unaugmented ὄλοντο used of the companions at 1.7. νόστιμον ἦμαρ is the formula of 1.9, where the Sun took the homecoming day from the companions; here it is Odysseus' own day, and his son says it is lost. The half-line ends the complaint, and the questions begin with the next verse.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον·
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon·
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: The whole line is the formula for turning to a question, and it comes again word for word at 206, in Athena's mouth; the English is the same both times. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is the epic 'come now', with the imperative ἄγε used as an interjection, as the plural ἄγετε is at 1.76. τόδε, 'this here', points forward to the questions. εἰπέ is the aorist imperative, as at 1.10. ἀτρεκέως, from ἀτρεκής, is 'without swerving, exactly'. κατάλεξον is the aorist imperative of καταλέγω, which in Homer is 'recount in full and in order', not 'choose'.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἰς ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.tr: tis pothen eis andrōn;
sentences.l: Who among men are you, and from where?
sentences.i: Who among men are you, and where from?
sentences.n: τίς and πόθεν stand side by side with no connective: two questions crowded into one. εἰς is the epic second singular of εἰμί (Attic εἶ). ἀνδρῶν is partitive with τίς, 'who of men'. Asking a guest his name and country once he has eaten is the regular thing to do, and Telemachus puts one question after another through 170 to 172 before he lets the stranger answer at all.

sentences.t: πόθι τοι πόλις ἠδὲ τοκῆες;
sentences.tr: pothi toi polis ēde tokēes;
sentences.l: Where is your city and your parents?
sentences.i: Where is your city, and where are your parents?
sentences.n: πόθι is 'where' (Attic ποῦ), with the suffix -θι of place where, against πόθεν 'from where' in the same line: the suffixes -θι, -θεν and -δε mark place where, place from and place to. τοι is the enclitic dative 'for you', a dative of the possessor: 'where is the city that is yours'. ἠδέ is the epic 'and'. τοκῆες is the nominative plural of τοκεύς 'parent', from τίκτω. The verb 'is' is left out again.

sentences.t: ὁπποίης τ’ ἐπὶ νηὸς ἀφίκεο·
sentences.tr: hoppoiēs t’ epi nēos aphikeo·
sentences.l: And on what sort of ship did you come?
sentences.i: And on what kind of ship did you come?
sentences.n: ὁπποίης is ὁποίας with the double π the verse wants, the indirect interrogative used directly, 'of what sort'; the Ionic η stands for Attic long α. νηός is the epic genitive of ναῦς (Attic νεώς). ἀφίκεο is an uncontracted second singular aorist middle (Attic ἀφίκου). The edition ends the clause with a raised point rather than a question mark, though the sense is a question like those on either side of it.

sentences.t:
πῶς δέ σε ναῦται
ἤγαγον εἰς Ἰθάκην;
sentences.tr:
pōs de se nautai
ēgagon eis Ithakēn;
sentences.l:
and how did sailors
bring you to Ithaca?
sentences.i: And how did sailors bring you to Ithaca?
sentences.n: ναῦται are the crew of the ship, and the question takes for granted that a man who reaches an island came in somebody's vessel. ἤγαγον is the reduplicated aorist of ἄγω, here with its augment. εἰς stands where ἐς has stood elsewhere in this part; Homer uses both forms. The question begins in the middle of 171 and stops in the middle of 172, as the two questions of 170 did.

sentences.t: τίνες ἔμμεναι εὐχετόωντο;
sentences.tr: tines emmenai euchetoōnto;
sentences.l: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.i: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.n: τίνες is the predicate of ἔμμεναι and so nominative, agreeing with the unexpressed subject of εὐχετόωντο. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι), as at 1.33. εὐχετόωντο is the imperfect of εὐχετάομαι with the vowel stretched back out, the diectasis seen in αἰτιόωνται at 1.32. The verb, like εὔχομαι, is 'declare oneself to be' rather than 'boast', and Athena answers with εὔχομαι at 180 and εὐχόμεθα at 187.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τί σε πεζὸν ὀίομαι ἐνθάδ’ ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti se pezon oiomai enthad’ hikesthai.
sentences.l: For in no way do I suppose that you came here on foot.
sentences.i: For I do not at all suppose that you came here on foot.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι: μέν is the emphatic particle, a weaker μήν with no answering δέ, as at 1.78, and οὔ τι is 'in no way'. πεζόν is predicative with σε, the subject of the infinitive, 'that you, on foot, came'. ὀίομαι 'suppose' is uncontracted. ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι. ἐνθάδε is 'here, to this place'. Ithaca is an island, and the remark is dry: it presses the question about the ship that has just been asked.

sentences.t:
καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐὺ εἰδῶ,
ἠὲ νέον μεθέπεις ἦ καὶ πατρώιός ἐσσι
ξεῖνος, ἐπεὶ πολλοὶ ἴσαν ἀνέρες ἡμέτερον δῶ
ἄλλοι, ἐπεὶ καὶ κεῖνος ἐπίστροφος ἦν ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr:
kai moi tout’ agoreuson etētymon, ophr’ ey eidō,
ēe neon methepeis ē kai patrōios essi
xeinos, epei polloi isan aneres hēmeteron dō
alloi, epei kai keinos epistrophos ēn anthrōpōn.
sentences.l:
And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well,
whether you come to us newly, or are also from my father's time
a guest-friend, since many men used to come to our house,
others, since that man too went about among people.”
sentences.i: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well: whether you are coming to us for the first time, or are a guest-friend from my father's time as well; for many other men used to come to our house, since he too went about among people.”
sentences.n: ἀγόρευσον is the aorist imperative of ἀγορεύω 'speak out', the verb Athena takes up at 179. ἐτήτυμον is an adverbial accusative, 'truly'. ὄφρα is the epic 'so that' with the subjunctive εἰδῶ; ἐύ is 'well' (Attic εὖ), printed without a diaeresis. ἠέ … ἦ is 'whether … or'. μεθέπεις, from μεθέπω 'come after', is 'you are coming to us', with νέον as an adverb, 'newly'. πατρώιος ξεῖνος is a guest-friend inherited from a father: ξενία bound two houses and passed to their sons. ἴσαν is the epic third plural imperfect of εἶμι. δῶ is an indeclinable epic word for a house.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is a third speech-introducing formula, beside τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα at 1.44 and 1.80 and τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη at 1.63; αὖτε, 'in turn', marks the exchange of speeches, and προσέειπε is the uncontracted aorist of προσεῖπον 'addressed' (Attic προσεῖπε). τόν is the pronoun, 'him'. The second half of the line, θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη, is exactly the half-line of 1.44 and 1.80 and is rendered the same way here.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι ταῦτα μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi tauta mal’ atrekeōs agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you these things very exactly.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you all of this quite exactly.
sentences.n: τοιγάρ, 'well then', is the particle for taking up a request and answering it. τοι is the enclitic dative 'to you', not the particle. μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως answers the ἀτρεκέως of the demand at 169, and ἀγορεύσω answers ἀγόρευσον at 174: she gives him his own words back. The future is a promise, and what she promises to tell exactly is, to begin with, an account of a man who does not exist: the narrator said at 105 that she had made herself like Mentes.

sentences.t:
Μέντης Ἀγχιάλοιο δαΐφρονος εὔχομαι εἶναι
υἱός, ἀτὰρ Ταφίοισι φιληρέτμοισιν ἀνάσσω.
sentences.tr:
Mentēs Anchialoio daïphronos euchomai einai
huios, atar Taphioisi philēretmoisin anassō.
sentences.l:
Mentes, of wise-minded Anchialus, I declare myself to be
the son, and I am lord over the oar-loving Taphians.
sentences.i: I declare myself to be Mentes, son of wise-hearted Anchialus, and I am lord over the oar-loving Taphians.
sentences.n: Μέντης is nominative as the predicate of εἶναι after εὔχομαι, which answers Telemachus' εὐχετόωντο at 172: 'I declare myself to be'. Ἀγχιάλοιο is a genitive in -οιο, and υἱός is held over to the head of 181. δαΐφρων is the epithet given to Odysseus at 1.48 and is kept as 'wise-minded' here too, a stock epithet being rendered the same way wherever it stands; the doubt about its sense is the same, 'skilled' from δαῆναι or 'warlike' from δάϊς. The name Ἀγχίαλος is 'near the sea', apt in a Taphian. φιλήρετμος is φίλος with ἐρετμόν 'oar'. ἀνάσσω takes the dative, as at 117.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὧδε ξὺν νηὶ κατήλυθον ἠδ’ ἑτάροισιν
πλέων ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον ἐπ’ ἀλλοθρόους ἀνθρώπους,
ἐς Τεμέσην μετὰ χαλκόν, ἄγω δ’ αἴθωνα σίδηρον.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ hōde xyn nēi katēlython ēd’ hetaroisin
pleōn epi oinopa ponton ep’ allothroous anthrōpous,
es Temesēn meta chalkon, agō d’ aithōna sidēron.
sentences.l:
And now I have put in here with my ship and my companions,
sailing over the wine-faced open-sea to men of other speech,
to Temese after bronze; and I carry fire-bright iron.
sentences.i: And now I have put in here with my ship and my companions, sailing over the sea that has the look of wine to men of another tongue, to Temese after bronze; and the cargo I carry is fire-bright iron.
sentences.n: ὧδε is 'here, to this place'. ξύν is the epic σύν. ἑτάροισιν is the shorter form of ἑταίροισιν, as at 1.6. κατήλυθον is the aorist of κατέρχομαι, used of putting in from the sea. οἶνοψ is οἶνος with ὄψ 'look, face', the second element of γλαυκῶπις: 'having the look of wine'. What colour is meant has never been settled, and the familiar English 'wine-dark' supplies a word the Greek does not have. ἀλλόθροος is ἄλλος with θρόος 'speech'. μετά with the accusative is 'in quest of'. αἴθων, from αἴθω 'kindle', is 'blazing, gleaming'; of iron the sense is disputed. Iron goes out and bronze is to come back.

sentences.t:
νηῦς δέ μοι ἥδ’ ἕστηκεν ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ νόσφι πόληος,
ἐν λιμένι Ῥείθρῳ ὑπὸ Νηίῳ ὑλήεντι.
sentences.tr:
nēus de moi hēd’ hestēken ep’ agrou nosphi polēos,
en limeni Rheithrōi hypo Nēiōi hylēenti.
sentences.l:
And this ship of mine lies at her moorings out in the country, away from the city,
in the harbour of Rheithron, below wooded Neion.
sentences.i: My ship lies at her moorings out in the country, away from the city, in the harbour of Rheithron, below wooded Neion.
sentences.n: νηῦς is the epic nominative of ναῦς. μοι is a dative of the possessor with ἥδε, 'this ship of mine'. ἕστηκεν is the perfect of ἵστημι with present sense, 'stands, is lying'. ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ is 'out in the fields', away from the town, the same phrase used of Laertes at 190. νόσφι with the genitive is 'apart from', as at 1.20. πόληος is the epic genitive of πόλις (Attic πόλεως). Ῥεῖθρον, 'stream', and Νήιον are places in Ithaca, named only here in this part. ὑλήεις is 'wooded', from ὕλη.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνοι δ’ ἀλλήλων πατρώιοι εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι
ἐξ ἀρχῆς,
sentences.tr:
xeinoi d’ allēlōn patrōioi euchometh’ einai
ex archēs,
sentences.l:
And we declare ourselves to be guest-friends of one another from our fathers' time,
from the beginning,
sentences.i: And we declare ourselves guest-friends of one another from our fathers' time, from the beginning,
sentences.n: This answers the second half of the question at 175 to 176, πατρώιός ἐσσι ξεῖνος, with the same two words in the plural. εὐχόμεθ’ is εὐχόμεθα, the verb of 180. ἀλλήλων is a genitive with ξεῖνοι: each is the other's guest-friend, and the bond is mutual and binding. ἐξ ἀρχῆς, 'from the start', is held over to the head of 188 and rounds off the claim, and the condition that follows begins in the middle of that line.

sentences.t:
εἴ πέρ τε γέροντ’ εἴρηαι ἐπελθὼν
Λαέρτην ἥρωα, τὸν οὐκέτι φασὶ πόλινδε
ἔρχεσθ’, ἀλλ’ ἀπάνευθεν ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ πήματα πάσχειν
γρηὶ σὺν ἀμφιπόλῳ,
sentences.tr:
ei per te geront’ eirēai epelthōn
Laertēn hērōa, ton ouketi phasi polinde
erchesth’, all’ apaneuthen ep’ agrou pēmata paschein
grēi syn amphipolōi,
sentences.l:
if indeed you should go and ask the old man,
Laertes the hero, who they say no longer to the city
comes, but far off in the country suffers woes
with an old woman as his attendant,
sentences.i: if indeed you were to go and ask the old man, Laertes the hero, who they say no longer comes to the city but is far off in the country, suffering hardship with an old woman for his attendant,
sentences.n: εἴ περ with the subjunctive εἴρηαι (an uncontracted second singular subjunctive middle of the epic εἴρομαι = ἔρομαι, Attic ἔρῃ) is 'if you were to ask', and τε here is the epic τε of a standing fact. ἐπελθών, 'having gone to him', is ἐλθών under another preverb, as μετελθών was at 134. Laertes, the father of Odysseus, is named for the first time. τόν is the article-form used as a relative, 'whom', and it is the subject of the two infinitives after φασί. πόλινδε has the suffix -δε 'to', like Ἰθάκηνδε at 163. ἀπάνευθεν is 'far off, apart'. πήματα πάσχειν is the phrase used of Odysseus himself at 1.49.

sentences.t:
ἥ οἱ βρῶσίν τε πόσιν τε
παρτιθεῖ, εὖτ’ ἄν μιν κάματος κατὰ γυῖα λάβῃσιν
ἑρπύζοντ’ ἀνὰ γουνὸν ἀλωῆς οἰνοπέδοιο.
sentences.tr:
hē hoi brōsin te posin te
partithei, eut’ an min kamatos kata guia labēisin
herpyzont’ ana gounon alōēs oinopedoio.
sentences.l:
who for him food and drink
sets beside him, whenever weariness takes hold of his limbs
as he creeps up the rising ground of his vineyard plot.
sentences.i: who sets food and drink beside him whenever weariness takes hold of his limbs as he creeps up the rising ground of his vineyard plot.
sentences.n: ἥ is the relative 'who', and οἱ the enclitic dative 'for him'. βρῶσις and πόσις are 'eating' and 'drinking', the pair that stood as ἐδητύς and πόσις at 150. παρτιθεῖ is παρατίθησι with the preposition cut short and an ending as of a contract verb. εὖτ’ ἄν with the subjunctive λάβῃσιν, ending in -ῃσι as at 1.77, is 'whenever'. κατὰ γυῖα goes with λάβῃσιν, 'takes him down through the limbs'. ἑρπύζοντ’ is ἑρπύζοντα, agreeing with μιν, from ἑρπύζω 'crawl'. γουνός is a rise of ground; οἰνόπεδος is 'wine-ground', a genitive in -οιο with ἀλωή, the planted plot.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἦλθον·
sentences.tr: nyn d’ ēlthon·
sentences.l: But now I have come;
sentences.i: But now I have come:
sentences.n: The half-line answers the first half of Telemachus' question at 175, ἠὲ νέον μεθέπεις: the friendship is old, but this visit is new. ἦλθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, here with its augment, and a Greek aorist of this kind answers to an English perfect. νῦν δέ is the same turn as at 166, 'but as things stand now'. The sentence is a half-line, and the reason follows in the second half of 194.

sentences.t:
δὴ γάρ μιν ἔφαντ’ ἐπιδήμιον εἶναι,
σὸν πατέρ’·
sentences.tr:
dē gar min ephant’ epidēmion einai,
son pater’·
sentences.l:
for indeed they said that he was at home,
your father;
sentences.i: for they told me that he was at home, your father;
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ gives the reason, 'for in fact'. μιν is 'him', the subject of the infinitive εἶναι, and σὸν πατέρ’ stands in apposition to it, held over to the head of 195 so that it falls last: she names the father only after she has said what she was told about him. ἔφαντ’ is ἔφαντο, the imperfect middle of φημί with its augment, 'they were saying', the middle used with the same force as the active, as at 1.42. ἐπιδήμιος is ἐπί with δῆμος, 'in his own district, at home'; δῆμος is the word used of Ithaca at 103.

sentences.t: ἀλλά νυ τόν γε θεοὶ βλάπτουσι κελεύθου.
sentences.tr: alla ny ton ge theoi blaptousi keleuthou.
sentences.l: but the gods, it seems, are baulking him of his way.
sentences.i: but the gods, it seems, are baulking him of his way.
sentences.n: νυ is the light particle 'now, then' of 1.32, and it gives the sentence a shrug. τόν γε is the pronoun, 'him at any rate'. βλάπτω in Homer is 'hinder, trip up' rather than the later 'harm', and it takes a genitive of separation, κελεύθου 'from his journey'. κέλευθος is a way or road, and of the sea a voyage. The speaker keeps up the manner of a trader who knows no more than common report; the reader has been told at 1.68 to 1.75 which god it is and why.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω τέθνηκεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἀλλ’ ἔτι που ζωὸς κατερύκεται εὐρέι πόντῳ
νήσῳ ἐν ἀμφιρύτῃ, χαλεποὶ δέ μιν ἄνδρες ἔχουσιν
ἄγριοι, οἵ που κεῖνον ἐρυκανόωσ’ ἀέκοντα.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō tethnēken epi chthoni dios Odysseus,
all’ eti pou zōos kateryketai eurei pontōi
nēsōi en amphirytēi, chalepoi de min andres echousin
agrioi, hoi pou keinon erykanoōs’ aekonta.
sentences.l:
For not yet has heavenly Odysseus died upon the earth,
but still, I suppose, alive he is held back on the wide open-sea,
on an island flowed-around, and harsh men hold him,
savage ones, who, I suppose, keep that man back against his will.
sentences.i: For heavenly Odysseus has not yet died upon the earth. He is still alive, I suppose, held back on the wide sea, on an island with the sea running all round it, and harsh men hold him, savage men who keep him back against his will.
sentences.n: δῖος belongs with Ζεύς and the bright sky, and it is the word rendered 'heavenly' in δῖα θεάων at 1.14; a stock epithet is kept the same way every time, even in a sentence about whether the man is dead. τέθνηκεν is the perfect of θνῄσκω; πω is 'yet'. κατερύκεται is the passive of the verb used of Calypso at 1.55. εὐρέι is the uncontracted dative of εὐρύς. νήσῳ ἐν ἀμφιρύτῃ repeats the phrase of 1.50 word for word. The harsh and savage men, on the other hand, are no part of the account Athena gave the gods there. ἐρυκανόωσ’ shows diectasis again; ἀέκοντα is ἄκοντα.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ νῦν τοι ἐγὼ μαντεύσομαι, ὡς ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ἀθάνατοι βάλλουσι καὶ ὡς τελέεσθαι ὀίω,
οὔτε τι μάντις ἐὼν οὔτ’ οἰωνῶν σάφα εἰδώς.
sentences.tr:
autar nyn toi egō manteusomai, hōs eni thymōi
athanatoi ballousi kai hōs teleesthai oiō,
oute ti mantis eōn out’ oiōnōn sapha eidōs.
sentences.l:
But now I will prophesy to you, as into my heart
the immortals put it, and as I think it will be brought about,
being neither a seer at all nor one who knows birds clearly.
sentences.i: But now I will prophesy to you, as the immortals put it into my heart, and as I think it will come about — and I am no seer, nor do I read birds with any certainty.
sentences.n: μαντεύσομαι is from μάντις, the professional seer, and the whole of 202 takes back what the verb claims. ὡς … βάλλουσι is 'as they put it', with ἐνὶ θυμῷ 'into my heart'; βάλλω is used of a thought dropped into a man's mind. τελέεσθαι is the uncontracted future middle infinitive of τελέω 'bring to pass' (Attic τελεῖσθαι), with ὀίω 'I think', the verb of 173. ἐών is the epic ὤν. An οἰωνός is a bird of omen, and reading the flight of birds is the commonest Greek way of taking a sign; σάφα is 'clearly, for certain'.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι ἔτι δηρόν γε φίλης ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης
ἔσσεται, οὐδ’ εἴ πέρ τε σιδήρεα δέσματ’ ἔχῃσιν·
sentences.tr:
ou toi eti dēron ge philēs apo patridos aiēs
essetai, oud’ ei per te sidērea desmat’ echēisin·
sentences.l:
Not for long yet, I tell you, from his dear fatherland
will he be, not even if bonds of iron hold him;
sentences.i: He will not be away from his dear fatherland much longer, not even if bonds of iron are holding him;
sentences.n: τοι is the particle here, 'I tell you', not the dative pronoun of 179. δηρόν is an adverbial accusative, 'for long', of the same family as δηθά at 120. In φίλης ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης the preposition stands inside its own phrase, between the adjective and the noun; αἶα is the by-form of γαῖα used at 1.41 and 1.75, and φίλης is 'his own dear'. ἔσσεται is ἔσται, as at 1.40, held over to the head of 204. σιδήρεα is uncontracted (Attic σιδηρᾶ) and picks up the σίδηρος of her cargo at 184. ἔχῃσιν is the subjunctive in -ῃσι seen at 192.

sentences.t: φράσσεται ὥς κε νέηται, ἐπεὶ πολυμήχανός ἐστιν.
sentences.tr: phrassetai hōs ke neētai, epei polymēchanos estin.
sentences.l: he will devise how he is to return, since he is many-devising.
sentences.i: He will devise a way to come back, for he is a man of many devices.
sentences.n: φράσσεται is the future middle of φράζομαι 'consider, devise', with the double σ the verse wants. ὥς κε νέηται is the whole phrase of 1.87, there 'that he is to return' after νόστον and here 'how he is to return' after φράσσεται, with κε for ἄν and the uncontracted νέομαι that shares its root with νόστος. πολυμήχανος is πολύς with μηχανή 'device, contrivance', a fourth compound epithet of Odysseus beside δαΐφρων, πολύφρων and ταλασίφρων, and like them it is kept distinct from the others. The line answers the iron bonds of 204: what holds him is nothing against what he can contrive.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
εἰ δὴ ἐξ αὐτοῖο τόσος πάϊς εἰς Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.tr:
all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon,
ei dē ex autoio tosos païs eis Odysēos.
sentences.l:
But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly,
whether indeed you are the son of Odysseus himself, grown so tall.
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly: whether you are indeed the son of Odysseus himself, grown so tall as you are.
sentences.n: Line 206 is 169 word for word, now turned back on the questioner, and the English of it is the same as there; a repeated line keeps its rendering. The comma at the end is the only difference the edition prints, since here the sentence runs on. εἰ δή introduces an indirect question after the imperatives, 'whether in fact'. ἐξ … Ὀδυσῆος is a genitive of descent, with αὐτοῖο (a genitive in -οιο of αὐτός) 'himself' and the name kept for the end of the line. τόσος is 'so big'. πάϊς is the uncontracted παῖς, and εἰς is 'you are', as at 170.

sentences.t:
αἰνῶς μὲν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ὄμματα καλὰ ἔοικας
κείνῳ, ἐπεὶ θαμὰ τοῖον ἐμισγόμεθ’ ἀλλήλοισιν,
πρίν γε τὸν ἐς Τροίην ἀναβήμεναι, ἔνθα περ ἄλλοι
Ἀργείων οἱ ἄριστοι ἔβαν κοίλῃς ἐνὶ νηυσίν·
sentences.tr:
ainōs men kephalēn te kai ommata kala eoikas
keinōi, epei thama toion emisgometh’ allēloisin,
prin ge ton es Troiēn anabēmenai, entha per alloi
Argeiōn hoi aristoi eban koilēis eni nēusin·
sentences.l:
Terribly, in your head and your fine eyes, you are like
that man, since often in this way we used to meet one another,
before he went up to Troy, where indeed the others,
the best of the Argives, went in hollow ships;
sentences.i: You are astonishingly like him about the head and the fine eyes, since we used often to meet in this way, before he went up to Troy, where the best of the Argives went too, in their hollow ships;
sentences.n: αἰνῶς is 'terribly', used of a likeness that is almost uncanny. κεφαλήν and ὄμματα are accusatives of respect with ἔοικας, the construction of ἐλαφρότεροι πόδας at 164, and κείνῳ is the dative ἔοικα takes. θαμά is 'often', the adverb of 143. τοῖον is adverbial, 'in such a way', that is, sitting and talking as these two are now. ἐμισγόμεθ’ is ἐμισγόμεθα, the imperfect middle of μίσγω with its augment. πρίν takes the infinitive ἀναβήμεναι, an infinitive in -μεναι; ἀναβαίνω ἐς is to go up from the coast to an inland place. ἔβαν is the epic third plural aorist (Attic ἔβησαν).

sentences.t: ἐκ τοῦ δ’ οὔτ’ Ὀδυσῆα ἐγὼν ἴδον οὔτ’ ἔμ’ ἐκεῖνος.
sentences.tr: ek tou d’ out’ Odysēa egōn idon out’ em’ ekeinos.
sentences.l: and from that time neither have I seen Odysseus nor he me.”
sentences.i: and from that time I have not seen Odysseus, nor he me.”
sentences.n: ἐκ τοῦ is 'from that time', the phrase of 1.74, where it could also be read 'for that reason'. ἐγών is ἐγώ in the form used before a vowel, as at 1.88. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist, as at 113, and it serves both halves of the sentence: in οὔτ’ ἔμ’ ἐκεῖνος the verb is not repeated. ἐκεῖνος stands here in full beside the shortened κεῖνος used at 163, 199 and 209. The line ends Athena's speech, and the English layers close their quotation marks here.
